newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says no to more Megawati protests.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says no to more Megawati protests.

text.p: Indonesian authorities will not tolerate any more protests by supporters of Megawati Sukarnoputri, the ousted leader of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), newspapers and the official Antara news agency reported on Thursday.

The Jakarta Post newspaper quoted armed forces spokesman Brigadier-General Slamet Supriadi as saying on Wednesday that authorities "would not hesitate to take stern action if Megawati loyalists went back onto the streets".

Hundreds of Megawati supporters held a six-hour demonstration in front of parliament house in Jakarta on Tuesday, blocking the main thoroughfare alongside and causing huge traffic jams in downtown areas.
Media Indonesia quoted Supriadi as saying that he regretted Tuesday's protest because it badly disrupted traffic.
"They should not have come in such a large numbers," Supriadi said. He was not available for comment.
Tuesday's demonstration was a show of strength in support of Megawati ahead of the May 29 general elections, organisers said.

She has been barred from participating in the polls because her name and those of her supporters were omitted from the list of election candidates supplied by the government-backed faction of her party which ousted her from the leadership last June.
Antara reported that police would take firm action against anyone violating the law ahead of the elections, including those holding demostrations.

"If they (the people) wish to convey their aspirations according to the regulations and are willing to preserve security in the capital city, then I would say go ahead," Jakarta Police Chief Major-General Hamami Nata was quoted as saying.
"Police will act firmly if they violate the law and commit destructive acts," said Nata, who was commenting on the demonstration staged by Megawati's supporters.
Indonesia only allows three parties to contest elections -- the PDI, the ruling Golkar and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party -- and election candidates must be approved by the government.
The government has said the PDI faction headed by Megawati's rivals constitutes the genuine wing of the party.

Jakarta was rocked by its worst riots in two decades when members of the government-backed faction stormed the PDI headquarters in the city in July and ousted Megawati supporters with the help of police. At least five people were killed and 149 injured in the violence.
A number of buildings were damaged and dozens of vehicles set on fire.
